question: What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?
answer: Semantic HTML uses elements that describe their meaning (header, nav, main, article, section, footer, aside, button) rather than generic divs/spans. It improves accessibility (screen readers understand structure), SEO (crawlers grasp content), and maintainability. Use the right element for the job—a button for actions, headings for hierarchy—so the document is meaningful to browsers, assistive tech, and developers.

question: What is the CSS box model?
answer: Every element is a box composed of content, padding (inside the border), border, and margin (outside). Total size depends on box-sizing: content-box (default—width is content only, padding/border add to it) vs border-box (width includes padding and border—more predictable). Most projects set box-sizing: border-box globally so widths are intuitive. Understanding the box model is fundamental to layout and spacing.

question: What is the difference between Flexbox and CSS Grid?
answer: Flexbox is one-dimensional—laying items along a row or column with flexible sizing/alignment—ideal for components, toolbars, and distributing space along one axis. Grid is two-dimensional—defining rows AND columns simultaneously—ideal for page/section layouts with precise placement. Use Flexbox for content flow in one direction and Grid for structured 2D layouts; they combine well (Grid for layout, Flex within cells).

question: How does CSS specificity work?
answer: Specificity determines which conflicting rule wins, scored by selector types: inline styles (highest), then IDs, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then elements/pseudo-elements. More specific selectors override less specific ones; ties are broken by source order (later wins). !important overrides normal specificity (avoid it). Keep specificity low and consistent (prefer classes, avoid deep nesting/IDs) to keep CSS maintainable and predictable.

question: What is the difference between position relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky?
answer: static is the default (normal flow). relative offsets an element from its normal position (and becomes a positioning context). absolute removes it from flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor. fixed positions relative to the viewport (stays on scroll). sticky toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll threshold (stays until its container scrolls out). Choose by whether the element should scroll, pin, or overlay.

question: How do you make a responsive design?
answer: Use fluid layouts (%, fr, flex/grid), relative units (rem/em, vw/vh), max-width with responsive images (max-width:100%), CSS media queries to adjust layout at breakpoints (mobile-first: base styles then min-width queries), and modern tools (container queries, clamp() for fluid typography). Test across viewport sizes. Design mobile-first and progressively enhance for larger screens for maintainable responsiveness.

question: What are CSS custom properties (variables)?
answer: CSS custom properties (--main-color: #333; used as var(--main-color)) are native variables that cascade and can be updated at runtime (via JS or media queries), unlike preprocessor variables that are compiled away. They enable theming (light/dark), consistent design tokens, and dynamic styling. Define them on :root for globals and override in scopes/themes. They're a foundation for maintainable, themeable CSS.

question: What is web accessibility (a11y) and ARIA?
answer: Accessibility ensures people with disabilities can use your site (keyboard navigation, screen readers, sufficient contrast, focus management). Use semantic HTML first (it's inherently accessible), then ARIA attributes (roles, aria-label, aria-expanded) to fill gaps for custom widgets—but only when needed ('no ARIA is better than bad ARIA'). Follow WCAG guidelines, test with keyboard and screen readers, and ensure color contrast and alt text. It's both ethical and often legally required.

question: What are Core Web Vitals?
answer: Core Web Vitals are Google's user-centric performance metrics: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint—loading, target <2.5s), INP (Interaction to Next Paint—responsiveness, replaced FID), and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift—visual stability, <0.1). They measure real user experience and affect SEO. Improve them by optimizing images/critical resources (LCP), minimizing main-thread blocking (INP), and reserving space for dynamic content (CLS).

question: How do you optimize frontend load performance?
answer: Minimize and split bundles (code splitting, lazy loading), tree-shake unused code, compress (gzip/brotli), optimize and lazy-load images (modern formats, responsive sizes), cache static assets via CDN with long cache headers, defer/async non-critical JS, inline critical CSS, preconnect/preload key resources, and reduce third-party scripts. Measure with Lighthouse. Prioritize the critical rendering path so users see content fast.

question: What is event delegation and why use it?
answer: Event delegation attaches a single listener to a common ancestor and uses event bubbling to handle events from many child elements (checking event.target), instead of adding a listener per child. Benefits: better performance/memory for large or dynamic lists, and it automatically handles elements added later. Use it for lists, tables, and dynamic content. It leverages the capturing/bubbling event flow.

question: What is the difference between event capturing and bubbling?
answer: When an event fires, it propagates in phases: capturing (from the root down to the target) then bubbling (from the target back up to the root). By default listeners run in the bubbling phase; pass {capture:true} to listen during capture. Bubbling enables event delegation. Use stopPropagation to halt propagation and preventDefault to cancel default behavior. Understanding the flow is key to handling nested element events.

question: What is the DOM and how do you update it efficiently?
answer: The DOM is the browser's tree representation of the page that JS can read/modify. Direct DOM manipulation is expensive (reflow/repaint), so update efficiently: batch changes (DocumentFragment), minimize layout thrashing (read then write, avoid interleaving reads/writes that force reflow), use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates, and let frameworks (React/Angular) diff and batch. Reducing reflows/repaints keeps the UI smooth.

question: What is a Web Worker and when do you use it?
answer: A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a background thread separate from the main UI thread, communicating via message passing (postMessage). Use it for CPU-intensive work (parsing large data, image processing, computations) that would otherwise freeze the UI, keeping the page responsive. Workers can't access the DOM directly. For heavy client-side processing (like building a large search index), offload to a worker.

question: What is CORS from the browser's perspective?
answer: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a browser security mechanism: by default, JS can't read responses from a different origin unless the server opts in via CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin, etc.). For non-simple requests the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request to check permissions. CORS errors are enforced by the browser, not the server. The fix is configuring the server's CORS policy—not disabling browser security.

question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies?
answer: localStorage persists data with no expiry until cleared (per origin, ~5-10MB, not sent to server). sessionStorage lasts for the tab session (cleared on tab close). Cookies (~4KB) are sent with every HTTP request to the origin, support expiry, and are used for server-side sessions/auth (with HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite flags). Use cookies for auth tokens (HttpOnly to prevent JS access), local/session storage for client-side non-sensitive state.

question: What is a Progressive Web App (PWA)?
answer: A PWA is a web app enhanced with native-like capabilities: installable (web app manifest), offline-capable and fast via a service worker (caching, background sync), push notifications, and responsive. Service workers are scriptable network proxies enabling offline and caching strategies. PWAs work across platforms from one codebase, offer app-like UX without app stores, and improve reliability on flaky networks.

question: What is the difference between defer and async on script tags?
answer: Both let the HTML parser continue while downloading the script (non-blocking). async executes the script as soon as it downloads, potentially out of order and interrupting parsing—good for independent scripts (analytics). defer waits until HTML parsing completes and executes in document order—good for scripts that depend on the DOM or each other. Prefer defer for app scripts to avoid blocking rendering and preserve order.

question: What is a type guard and narrowing in TypeScript?
answer: A type guard is a runtime check that narrows a union type to a specific type within a block: typeof (typeof x === 'string'), instanceof, 'in' checks, and custom user-defined guards (function isCat(a): a is Cat). After the check, TypeScript knows the narrower type, giving safe access to its members. Narrowing lets you work with unions and unknown safely, and enables exhaustive handling with discriminated unions.

question: What are enums vs union of literals in TypeScript?
answer: An enum defines named constants (enum Status { Active, Inactive }) producing a runtime object. A union of string literals (type Status = 'active' | 'inactive') is compile-time only, tree-shakable, and often preferred—more flexible, no runtime overhead, and works well with discriminated unions. Use literal unions for most cases; enums when you need a runtime object or numeric values. const enums inline values but have caveats.

question: What is memoization and how do you implement it in JS?
answer: Memoization caches a pure function's results keyed by arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs return the cached value instead of recomputing. Implement with a closure holding a Map: check the cache, compute on miss, store, return. Use it for expensive, deterministic computations (fibonacci, parsing). Beware unbounded cache growth (add size limits/LRU) and only memoize pure functions. React's useMemo/useCallback apply the concept to renders.

question: What is the difference between deep and shallow equality in JS?
answer: Shallow equality compares references for objects/arrays (=== ) and values for primitives—two structurally-identical objects are not shallow-equal. Deep equality compares nested contents recursively. React and many libraries use shallow comparison for performance (memo, dependency arrays), which is why creating new objects each render breaks memoization. Use deep comparison (lodash isEqual, structuredClone for copies) only when necessary—it's costlier.

question: What are Promises chaining and error handling patterns?
answer: Chain .then() to sequence async steps (each returning a value or promise), and .catch() to handle any rejection in the chain (errors propagate to the nearest catch), with .finally() for cleanup. With async/await, use try/catch/finally for the same. Always handle rejections to avoid unhandled promise rejections. For parallel independent work use Promise.all; for sequencing dependent steps, chain or await in order.

question: What is the difference between em, rem, %, vw/vh, and px?
answer: px is an absolute pixel. em is relative to the element's own font-size (compounds with nesting). rem is relative to the root font-size (predictable, good for scalable typography/spacing). % is relative to the parent's corresponding property. vw/vh are relative to viewport width/height (responsive sizing). Prefer rem for typography/spacing (accessibility—respects user font settings) and viewport units/% for responsive layout.

question: What is the difference between == null check and explicit undefined/null checks?
answer: x == null (loose equality) is true for both null and undefined (and only those), a common idiom to check 'no value'. x === null or x === undefined check exactly one. Use x == null to handle both absence cases concisely, or optional chaining/nullish coalescing (x ?? default) for defaults. Avoid other == coercions; == null is the one broadly-accepted loose-equality use.

question: What is the difference between inline, block, and inline-block elements?
answer: Block elements (div, p, section) start on a new line and take full available width, respecting width/height/margins. Inline elements (span, a, strong) flow within text, only take their content's width, and ignore width/height and vertical margins. inline-block flows inline (sits next to others) but respects width/height/margins like a block—useful for buttons/badges laid out horizontally with sizing. display controls this behavior.

question: What is a stacking context and z-index?
answer: z-index controls the front-to-back ordering of positioned elements, but only within the same stacking context. A stacking context is formed by certain properties (position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, etc.); child z-index values are contained within their parent's context. This is why a high z-index sometimes doesn't bring an element to front—it's trapped in a lower-stacked context. Understand stacking contexts to debug overlay/layering issues.

question: What is the difference between visibility hidden, display none, and opacity 0?
answer: display:none removes the element from layout entirely (no space, not rendered, not accessible). visibility:hidden hides it but keeps its space in layout (invisible but occupies room). opacity:0 makes it fully transparent but still occupies space AND remains interactive (clickable). Choose display:none to remove, visibility:hidden to hide while preserving layout, and opacity for transitions/fades (often with pointer-events:none to disable interaction).

question: What is the difference between fetch and XMLHttpRequest?
answer: fetch is the modern promise-based API for HTTP requests—cleaner syntax, streaming support, and integrates with async/await. XMLHttpRequest (XHR) is the older callback/event-based API—more verbose but supports upload progress events (which fetch lacks natively) and older browser support. Use fetch for most modern code (with AbortController for cancellation/timeout); XHR mainly for progress tracking or legacy needs. Libraries (axios) wrap either with extra features.

question: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks with an example?
answer: After each macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, event), the event loop drains ALL pending microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) before the next macrotask or render. So Promise.resolve().then(...) runs before a setTimeout(...,0) scheduled earlier. Example: console.log('a'); setTimeout(()=>log('b')); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log('c')); log('d') prints a, d, c, b—sync first, then microtask c, then macrotask b.

question: What is critical rendering path optimization?
answer: The critical rendering path is the sequence the browser follows to turn HTML/CSS/JS into pixels (parse HTML→DOM, CSS→CSSOM, JS execution, render tree, layout, paint). Optimize it by minimizing render-blocking resources: inline critical CSS, defer/async non-critical JS, reduce CSS/JS size, preload key resources, and avoid layout thrashing. Getting content to first paint fast (fewer round-trips, smaller critical resources) improves perceived load and Core Web Vitals.

question: How do you make a custom component keyboard accessible?
answer: Ensure it's focusable (tabindex=0 for custom interactive elements, or use native button/a), handle keyboard events (Enter/Space to activate, arrow keys for menus/tabs per ARIA patterns), manage focus (move focus into modals, trap it, restore on close), provide visible focus indicators, and add appropriate ARIA roles/states (role, aria-expanded, aria-selected). Prefer native semantic elements which are accessible by default; only add ARIA/JS when building custom widgets.

question: How does CSS specificity work and why is important a smell?
answer: Specificity ranks inline styles above ids above classes above elements, with the last matching rule winning ties. important overrides all of it, so it wins today and forces the next override to escalate, ending in an unmaintainable arms race. The fix is lowering specificity - single classes, layers, or custom properties - rather than raising it.

question: What are container queries and what do they solve that media queries do not?
answer: Media queries respond to the viewport, so a component cannot know it is in a narrow sidebar on a wide screen. Container queries respond to the size of an ancestor container, letting a component adapt to the space it actually occupies. That is what makes truly reusable responsive components possible in a design system.

question: What is the difference between rem, em, px and viewport units?
answer: px is absolute and ignores user font preferences. em is relative to the element's font size and compounds through nesting. rem is relative to the root, giving predictable scaling that respects browser font settings. Viewport units scale with the window, useful for hero sections but dangerous for text, which can become unreadably small or large.

question: What is semantic HTML and what does it actually buy you?
answer: Using elements for their meaning - nav, main, button, heading levels - gives assistive technology structure to navigate, gives search engines context, and brings built-in keyboard and focus behaviour for free. A div with a click handler has none of that, which is why rebuilding a button correctly takes far more code than using one.

question: What are the WCAG levels and which criteria matter most in practice?
answer: A, AA and AAA, with AA the usual legal and contractual target. In practice the high-impact criteria are colour contrast, keyboard operability of every interactive element, visible focus indication, form labels and error identification, and meaningful alternative text. Those cover the majority of real barriers users encounter.

question: What is the difference between aria-label, aria-labelledby and a visible label?
answer: A visible label associated with the control is best because it helps everyone, including users with cognitive difficulties and voice control. aria-labelledby points to existing visible text. aria-label supplies an invisible name and should be a last resort, since it can diverge from the visible text and break voice-control users who say what they see.

question: How do you test accessibility beyond an automated scan?
answer: Automated tools catch perhaps a third of issues - contrast, missing labels, invalid ARIA. The rest needs manual work: navigate the whole flow with the keyboard only, use a screen reader for the critical journey, zoom to 200 percent, and check that focus order and announcements make sense. Include users with disabilities where possible.

question: What causes cumulative layout shift and how do you prevent it?
answer: Images and iframes without dimensions, ads and embeds injected above content, web fonts swapping at a different size, and content inserted after load. Prevent it by reserving space with width and height or aspect-ratio, using font-display with a metric-matched fallback, and inserting dynamic content below the fold or in reserved containers.

question: How do you optimise web font loading?
answer: Subset to the characters you need, self-host with a long cache lifetime, preload the fonts used above the fold, use font-display swap or optional, and pick a fallback whose metrics are adjusted with size-adjust so the swap does not shift layout. Loading several weights and styles unnecessarily is the most common waste.

question: What image format and loading choices matter most for performance?
answer: Serve AVIF or WebP with a fallback, size images to the largest rendered dimension rather than the original, use responsive srcset with sizes, lazy-load below-the-fold images, and mark the hero image high priority so it is not delayed. Images are usually the largest share of page weight, so this outranks most JavaScript tuning.

question: What is the difference between a CDN cache hit, a browser cache hit and a service worker cache hit?
answer: A browser cache hit costs nothing and never leaves the device. A service worker hit is programmable and works offline but runs JavaScript first. A CDN hit avoids the origin but still costs a network round trip. Cache-Control, ETag and immutable asset URLs are what determine which of these you get.

question: What is cache busting and how do content hashes solve it?
answer: Long cache lifetimes are only safe if the URL changes when the content does. Build tools embed a content hash in asset filenames, so a changed file gets a new URL and an unchanged one keeps its cached copy. The HTML referencing them must then be short-cached or revalidated, otherwise clients never learn about the new names.

question: Why does a sticky element sometimes not stick?
answer: Sticky requires a threshold such as top to be set, a scrolling ancestor, and no ancestor with overflow hidden, auto or scroll that clips it - and it sticks only within its parent's bounds, so a short parent means it stops early. Those four conditions cover nearly every reported failure.

question: What is the box model and what does box-sizing change?
answer: Width by default applies to the content box, with padding and border added outside it, so an element with a set width plus padding is wider than declared. box-sizing border-box makes width include padding and border, which is why almost every stylesheet sets it globally.

question: What causes margin collapsing and when is it a problem?
answer: Adjacent vertical margins between block elements combine into the larger rather than summing, and a parent with no padding or border collapses with its first or last child's margin. It surprises people as unexpected space outside a container, and is avoided with padding, a border, or a flex or grid formatting context.

question: How do CSS cascade layers change specificity management?
answer: Layers establish an explicit order so styles in a later layer beat earlier ones regardless of selector specificity. That lets a design system's base styles sit in a lower layer than application overrides, removing the specificity arms race and the need for important as an escape hatch.

question: How do you build a responsive layout without media queries?
answer: Use intrinsic techniques - flex wrap with a basis, grid with auto-fit and minmax, clamp for fluid typography and spacing, and container queries for component-level adaptation. These respond to available space continuously rather than at fixed breakpoints, which handles cases the breakpoint set never anticipated.

question: What is the difference between min-content, max-content and fit-content?
answer: min-content is the smallest width without overflow, typically the longest word. max-content is the width if nothing wrapped. fit-content clamps the max-content size to the available space. They allow sizing based on content rather than arbitrary pixel values, which is what makes grid tracks flexible without magic numbers.

question: Which CSS properties are cheap to animate and why?
answer: transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor without layout or paint, so they animate smoothly even under main-thread load. Animating width, top, or box-shadow triggers layout or paint on every frame. will-change can promote a layer, but overusing it consumes memory and can make things worse.

question: What is the difference between reflow and repaint?
answer: Reflow recalculates geometry and cascades to affected elements, which is the expensive one; repaint redraws pixels without changing layout. Composite-only changes skip both. Batching DOM reads and writes prevents forcing synchronous reflows, which is the main practical lever available to application code.

question: What does content-visibility do?
answer: It lets the browser skip rendering work for off-screen elements until they are needed, with contain-intrinsic-size supplying a placeholder height so scrollbars behave. On long pages it can substantially reduce initial rendering cost, at the risk of layout shift if the intrinsic size is badly estimated.

question: How do you measure real user performance rather than lab performance?
answer: Collect field data with the web-vitals library reporting to your analytics, segmented by device class, connection and page type, and look at the 75th percentile rather than the mean. Lab tools give a controlled comparison and diagnostics, but only field data reflects the devices your users actually have.

question: What is a performance budget and how do you enforce one?
answer: A limit on a measurable quantity - JavaScript bytes, largest contentful paint, request count - checked in CI against the build or a synthetic run, failing the build when exceeded. Without enforcement, budgets are aspirations, and page weight only ever moves in one direction.

question: What is the difference between the capture and bubble phases of an event?
answer: An event travels down from the root to the target in the capture phase, then back up in the bubble phase, with listeners defaulting to bubble. Capture is useful for intercepting before a child handles it - closing a menu on any outside click - and stopPropagation in either phase halts the rest of the journey.

question: What is the difference between requestAnimationFrame and setTimeout for animation?
answer: requestAnimationFrame runs before the next paint, synchronised with the display refresh, and pauses in background tabs - so animation is smooth and does not waste battery. A timer runs on its own schedule, producing dropped or doubled frames and continuing to run when nothing is visible.

question: What is the ResizeObserver and why is it better than a resize listener?
answer: It reports size changes of specific elements, including those caused by content or layout rather than window resizing, and it batches callbacks to avoid layout thrashing. A window resize listener misses element-level changes entirely and fires far more often than needed.

question: What are the practical limits of localStorage and what should replace it?
answer: Roughly five to ten megabytes per origin, synchronous so large reads block the main thread, string-only requiring serialisation, and unavailable in some privacy modes. IndexedDB is the alternative for anything sizeable or structured, and the Cache API for network responses.

question: How does the browser decide to cache a response?
answer: From Cache-Control directives - max-age, no-cache which means revalidate rather than never cache, no-store which means never write it down - plus validators such as ETag and Last-Modified for conditional requests. Misunderstanding no-cache as no-store is one of the most common caching mistakes.

question: What is the difference between a hard refresh, a normal refresh and a navigation?
answer: A navigation uses the cache normally. A refresh revalidates the main document and often subresources. A hard refresh bypasses the cache entirely. That difference is why a bug reproduces for users but not for the developer who keeps hard-refreshing, and why cache issues need testing with a normal navigation.

question: What is the accessibility tree and how does it relate to the DOM?
answer: The browser derives an accessibility tree from the DOM, exposing roles, names, states and relationships to assistive technology. Elements hidden with display none are excluded; ARIA attributes modify nodes. Inspecting it in devtools is the reliable way to check what a screen reader will actually announce.

question: What is the correct way to hide content visually but keep it available to screen readers?
answer: A visually-hidden utility class that clips the element to a single pixel with overflow hidden, rather than display none or visibility hidden which remove it from the accessibility tree. It is used for skip links, field descriptions and status text that has a visual equivalent elsewhere.

question: When should you use ARIA and when should you not?
answer: Only when native HTML cannot express the semantics. The first rule of ARIA is not to use ARIA - a button element already has the role, keyboard behaviour and focus handling that a div with role button must reimplement. Incorrect ARIA is worse than none because it overrides correct native semantics.

question: What are the WCAG contrast requirements and what do they apply to?
answer: Level AA requires 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text and for meaningful non-text elements such as icons, focus indicators and form borders. Placeholder text, disabled controls and decorative graphics have different treatment - and the common failure is grey secondary text that fails at small sizes.

question: How should keyboard focus be handled in a single-page application?
answer: After a route change, move focus to the new page's heading or main landmark and announce the change, since no page load occurs to reset it. Keep focus visible, never remove the outline without a replacement, and return focus to the trigger when a dialog closes.

question: How do you make a data table accessible?
answer: Use real table markup with header cells scoped to rows or columns, a caption describing the table, and avoid layout tables entirely. For complex tables, associate headers explicitly. Sortable columns need their state announced, and horizontally scrolling tables need a focusable container so keyboard users can scroll them.

question: What is subresource integrity and when should you use it?
answer: A hash attribute on a script or stylesheet tag so the browser refuses to execute the resource if its content does not match. It protects against a compromised CDN serving altered code. It requires updating the hash whenever the resource changes, which is why it suits pinned versions rather than floating ones.

question: Why is target blank without rel noopener a security issue?
answer: The opened page can access window.opener and navigate the original tab to a phishing page. Modern browsers default to noopener for target blank, but explicitly setting rel noopener noreferrer remains correct for older browsers and for links opened programmatically.

question: What risks come with third-party scripts on a page?
answer: They execute with full access to the DOM, cookies accessible to JavaScript, and any data on the page, so an analytics or chat widget compromise becomes your breach. Mitigate with a strict CSP, subresource integrity, sandboxed iframes where possible, and a genuine review of how many are actually needed.

question: What is a source map and what are the risks of shipping one?
answer: It maps minified code back to source so stack traces and debugging are readable. Publishing it publicly exposes your original source, including comments and any embedded secrets. The common approach is to generate them and upload to the error tracker without serving them from the public site.

question: How do you decide which browsers to support?
answer: From analytics of actual visitors rather than a generic list, expressed as a browserslist query that drives transpilation, polyfilling and CSS prefixing. Supporting an old browser has a real cost in bundle size for everyone, so the decision should be reviewed against traffic and revenue rather than inherited.

question: What is differential serving and is it still worth doing?
answer: Shipping a modern bundle to capable browsers and a transpiled one to older ones, selected with module and nomodule attributes. It was worth significant bundle savings when older browsers were common; with modern baselines, targeting recent browsers directly is usually simpler and gives most of the benefit.

question: How do you handle environment configuration in a static frontend build?
answer: Values are inlined at build time, so a single artifact cannot be promoted across environments unless configuration is fetched at runtime from an endpoint or injected into the served HTML. Choose deliberately - build-time is simpler, runtime is what allows one image to run everywhere.

question: How do you decide between server rendering and a single-page application?
answer: By what the page needs: content-heavy, SEO-relevant and first-visit-dominated pages favour server rendering; highly interactive, session-long applications favour client rendering. Most products need both, which is why frameworks converged on per-route or per-component rendering decisions rather than one global choice.

question: What is islands architecture?
answer: The page is server-rendered static HTML with small independently hydrated interactive regions, so JavaScript is loaded only for the parts that need it. It suits content sites with isolated interactivity and fits poorly where the whole page is one interactive application sharing state.

question: How do you handle shared state between micro-frontends?
answer: Minimise it - the point of the split is independence. Where it is unavoidable, use a well-defined contract such as custom events, a small shared store with a versioned interface, or the URL. Sharing a framework store instance couples the fragments to one framework version and defeats the architecture.

question: What is a BFF in frontend terms and what problem does it solve?
answer: A backend dedicated to one frontend, aggregating and reshaping downstream calls so the client makes one request for a screen rather than five. It solves over-fetching, chattiness on mobile networks, and keeping credentials off the client - and it gives the frontend team a backend they can change at their own pace.

question: Where should a frontend handle authorisation?
answer: For user experience only - hiding actions the user cannot take. Every enforcement decision belongs on the server, because the client is fully modifiable by the user. A frontend that hides an admin button while the API accepts the call from anyone has no authorisation at all.

question: How do you structure API calls in a frontend codebase?
answer: A thin transport layer handling base URL, auth, errors and retries; typed client functions per endpoint derived from the specification where possible; and feature-level hooks or services that use them. Scattering fetch calls through components makes cross-cutting changes - a new header, an error convention - a search-and-replace exercise.

question: What are the standard loading state patterns and when does each apply?
answer: A spinner for short waits, a skeleton matching the eventual layout for content that takes longer, optimistic rendering when the outcome is near-certain, and progressive display when parts arrive separately. Skeletons reduce perceived wait because the layout does not shift when content arrives.

question: How should a frontend handle an unexpected error?
answer: Show a clear message in user terms with an action - retry, go back, contact support with a reference - rather than a stack trace or a blank screen, log it with context to an error tracker, and preserve any unsaved work. The reference identifier is what turns a support conversation into a diagnosable incident.

question: What is optimistic UI and when is it inappropriate?
answer: Rendering the expected result immediately and reconciling when the server responds. It is inappropriate when failure is likely, when the operation is financially or legally significant, or when reverting would be confusing - a message appearing sent and then vanishing is worse than a brief spinner.

question: How do you handle offline or unreliable network conditions?
answer: Detect connectivity, queue mutations locally and replay when online, serve cached content for reads, and communicate state clearly rather than silently failing. Full offline support is a substantial commitment involving conflict resolution, so most applications should aim for graceful degradation instead.

question: What is the difference between debouncing a search input and cancelling requests?
answer: Debouncing reduces how many requests are sent; cancellation ensures a superseded response cannot overwrite a newer one. Both are needed - debouncing alone still leaves races when responses return out of order, and cancellation alone sends far more requests than necessary.

question: What determines whether a dependency ends up in the initial bundle?
answer: Whether it is statically imported from a module reachable from the entry point. A dynamic import creates a separate chunk loaded on demand. A single static import of a heavy library from a shared utility file is the usual reason a large dependency appears in the initial bundle unexpectedly.

question: How do you audit and reduce third-party JavaScript?
answer: Inventory every tag and script, measure its cost with the coverage tool and by removing it in a test, load non-critical ones after interaction or lazily, and challenge whether each is still needed. Marketing and analytics scripts accumulate silently and often exceed the application bundle.

question: What is the difference between a polyfill and a ponyfill?
answer: A polyfill patches the global environment so existing code works; a ponyfill exports the functionality for explicit import without modifying globals. Ponyfills avoid conflicts with other libraries and with a native implementation arriving later, which is why library authors prefer them.

question: How do you handle a dependency that only works in the browser during a server build?
answer: Import it dynamically inside a browser-only code path, guard with an environment check before the import, or configure the bundler to externalise it for the server build. A static top-level import executes on the server and fails at the first reference to a browser global.

question: What is the difference between jsdom and a real browser for tests?
answer: jsdom implements the DOM APIs without a rendering engine, so it is fast but has no layout, no real CSS, no paint and approximate event behaviour. It suits logic and structural assertions; anything depending on visual layout, scrolling, or genuine pointer interaction needs a real browser.

question: How do you test something that depends on element size or position?
answer: Inject the measurement so it can be stubbed in unit tests, and cover the real behaviour in a browser-based test at a fixed viewport. Mocking getBoundingClientRect in jsdom produces tests that pass while the real layout is broken, which is worse than not testing it there at all.

question: What should a smoke test for a frontend deployment check?
answer: That the page loads without console errors, the main bundle and assets resolve, authentication works, one representative data call succeeds, and a core interaction completes. It catches broken asset paths, misconfigured environment values and expired credentials - the failures that only appear once deployed.

question: How do you find what is blocking the main thread on page load?
answer: Record a performance profile and look at the main thread flame chart for long tasks, attributing them to script evaluation, parsing, or layout. Common culprits are a large bundle evaluating, synchronous third-party scripts, and expensive initial rendering of a long list before any virtualisation applies.

question: What is hydration cost and how do you reduce it?
answer: After server-rendered HTML arrives, the client must download, parse and execute the framework and components to attach behaviour, during which the page looks ready but is unresponsive. Reduce it by shipping less client JavaScript - server components, islands, partial or progressive hydration - rather than by optimising the hydration itself.

question: When does prefetching harm performance?
answer: When it competes with critical resources for bandwidth on a slow connection, when it prefetches paths users rarely take, or when it warms caches that are invalidated before use. Prefetch on interaction intent such as hover or viewport proximity rather than eagerly, and respect data saver preferences.

question: How do you make a long list feel fast without virtualisation?
answer: Paginate or use progressive loading, render a smaller initial page and expand on demand, keep row rendering cheap by avoiding per-row expensive components, and defer non-visible work with content-visibility. Virtualisation is the right answer above a few thousand rows, but these help earlier and cost less complexity.

question: What state belongs in the URL?
answer: Anything that should survive a refresh, be shareable, or participate in browser history - the current view, selected item, filters, sort, pagination, and open tab. Keeping it in component state means a shared link does not reproduce what the sender saw, which is a recurring source of support confusion.

question: How do you persist state across sessions responsibly?
answer: Store only what improves the experience - drafts, preferences, last viewed - with a version so a schema change does not break the application on the stored shape, an expiry, and no sensitive data. Restoring arbitrary application state from storage without validation is how a corrupt entry makes the app unloadable.

question: How do you keep state consistent across browser tabs?
answer: Listen to storage events or use a BroadcastChannel to notify other tabs of changes such as login, logout and preference updates. Without it, a user logging out in one tab remains apparently logged in elsewhere, and two tabs can write conflicting state to the same key.

question: What is the practical risk of storing a token in localStorage?
answer: Any script running on the page can read it, so a single XSS - including from a compromised third-party script - exfiltrates a valid credential. The mitigations are avoiding JavaScript-accessible tokens entirely with HttpOnly cookies, and a strict CSP that makes injected script execution difficult.

question: How do you safely render user-generated markdown?
answer: Render to HTML with a parser configured to disallow raw HTML, then sanitise the output with a maintained library, restricting tags, attributes and URL schemes - javascript URLs in links are the commonly missed vector. Do the sanitisation on the server or on both sides, never only in the client.

question: What is the risk of dynamically constructing URLs from user input?
answer: Open redirects that facilitate phishing, javascript scheme injection when the value becomes an href, and SSRF if the value reaches a server-side fetch. Validate against an allow-list of paths or hosts rather than filtering known-bad patterns, and never redirect to a URL supplied in a query parameter without validation.

question: How do you keep a design system and application in sync?
answer: Version the system as a package with semantic versioning and a changelog, publish a component catalogue with usage examples, provide codemods for breaking changes, and track adoption per consuming application. Without a migration path, applications pin an old version and the system fragments.

question: What belongs in a component's documentation?
answer: What it is for and when not to use it, the props with types and defaults, accessibility behaviour and requirements, examples of the common variants, and known limitations. A generated prop table alone does not tell a consumer which of five similar components to choose, which is the question they actually have.

question: How do you manage feature flags in a frontend application?
answer: Evaluate flags server-side where possible so the client does not download code for features it cannot use, provide defaults for when the flag service is unavailable, avoid layout shift from late evaluation, and remove flags promptly - stale flags multiply the states you must test.

question: How do you handle internationalisation beyond translating strings?
answer: Plural rules, date, number and currency formatting per locale, text expansion of up to a third affecting layout, right-to-left support, sorting and search collation, and avoiding string concatenation that assumes word order. Extracting strings is the easy part; the layout and grammar consequences are where projects underestimate.

question: How should a frontend report errors and performance to a backend service?
answer: Batch and send asynchronously with the beacon API so reporting does not block unload, include release version and user context without personal data, sample high-volume events, and fail silently if reporting fails. Reporting that itself throws or blocks navigation is a self-inflicted problem.

question: What is a sensible strategy for browser console errors in production?
answer: Capture them with a global handler and unhandled rejection handler, forward to an error tracker with source maps uploaded privately, group by fingerprint, and alert on new or spiking errors rather than on volume. An error console nobody watches is the same as no error handling.

question: How do you approach a frontend performance budget conversation with stakeholders?
answer: Translate to outcomes they care about - conversion, bounce rate, search ranking - cite field data for your own users rather than generic studies, and present the budget as protecting a measured business metric. Framing it as a technical preference is why budgets get overridden by the next marketing tag.

question: What is the difference between grid-template-areas and explicit line placement?
answer: Named areas make the layout readable in the stylesheet and easy to rearrange per breakpoint; line placement is more precise for irregular or dynamic layouts. Areas are usually clearer for page-level structure, and line-based placement is needed when items are positioned programmatically.

question: How does the aspect-ratio property help with layout stability?
answer: It reserves space proportionally before an image or embed loads, preventing the layout shift that occurs when the element suddenly gains height. It replaces the padding-percentage hack and works for any element, which makes reserving space for media a one-line concern rather than a wrapper structure.

question: What are logical properties in CSS and why use them?
answer: Properties expressed relative to the writing direction - inline-start rather than left - so a layout adapts automatically to right-to-left languages. Using them from the start removes an entire retrofit project when internationalisation reaches a right-to-left locale.

question: When should you use CSS nesting or a preprocessor now that both exist?
answer: Native nesting covers the common structural case with no build step. Preprocessors still offer loops, functions and mixins, though custom properties and modern CSS features have absorbed much of that. New projects can often start with plain CSS plus custom properties and add tooling only when a genuine gap appears.

question: What is the difference between a progressive web app and a native app in practical terms?
answer: A PWA installs from the web with no store review, updates instantly, and shares one codebase, but has restricted access to device capabilities and platform integrations that vary by browser. Native gives full capability and platform presence at the cost of separate codebases and release cycles.

question: What does a web app manifest control?
answer: The installed application's name, icons, theme colours, display mode and start URL. It is what makes a site installable and determines whether it opens in a browser chrome or standalone window. Getting the start URL and scope wrong is why an installed app sometimes opens the wrong page or falls out of standalone mode.

question: How do push notifications work on the web?
answer: A service worker subscribes to a push service, the server sends an encrypted payload to that endpoint, and the worker displays a notification. Permission must be requested in a user gesture and is easily denied permanently, so asking at the right moment with clear value matters more than the technical implementation.

question: What is the difference between the Cache API and HTTP caching?
answer: HTTP caching is managed by the browser according to headers; the Cache API is programmatic storage a service worker controls explicitly, with your own naming and eviction. The Cache API enables offline and custom strategies, at the cost of you owning invalidation entirely.

question: How do you handle authentication in end-to-end tests?
answer: Log in once programmatically, save the storage state, and reuse it across tests rather than driving the login form each time. That removes minutes from the suite and a common source of flakiness, while keeping one test that actually exercises the login flow.

question: How do you make end-to-end tests independent of test data state?
answer: Create the data each test needs through the API before the test and clean up after, using unique identifiers so parallel runs do not collide. Relying on a seeded shared dataset means tests break each other and a manual change in the environment silently invalidates the suite.

question: How do you handle browser-specific bugs?
answer: Reproduce with a minimal case, check whether it is a known issue with a documented workaround, apply a targeted fix behind feature detection rather than user-agent sniffing, and record why the workaround exists so it can be removed. Undocumented browser hacks outlive the bug by years.

question: What is feature detection and why is it preferred over user-agent sniffing?
answer: Testing whether a capability exists rather than inferring it from the browser identity. It stays correct as browsers gain features and as user agents lie or change format, and it handles the browser you never tested. User-agent checks are a maintenance liability from the day they are written.

question: How do you deprecate a component in a design system?
answer: Mark it deprecated in code and documentation with the replacement named, emit a development-time warning, provide a codemod where the migration is mechanical, track remaining usage, and remove only when usage reaches zero. Removing on a version bump without those steps breaks consumers who never saw the notice.

question: How do you decide what to preload, prefetch and preconnect?
answer: Preload resources needed for the current page's critical render - the hero image, the font. Prefetch resources for a likely next navigation. Preconnect to origins you will definitely use so the connection cost is paid early. Overusing any of them competes with the critical path for bandwidth.

question: What is the difference between compression and minification?
answer: Minification removes characters the parser does not need - whitespace, comments, long names - reducing the source size. Compression such as Brotli encodes the bytes for transfer and is undone by the browser. They compose: minified code compresses better, and both are needed for the smallest transfer.

question: What is a skip link and why does it matter?
answer: A link at the top of the page, usually visible only on focus, jumping to the main content so keyboard and screen reader users bypass repeated navigation. Without it, every page requires tabbing through the entire header, which is the most common complaint in keyboard accessibility reviews.

question: How do you make an error summary accessible?
answer: Render a summary at the top listing each error as a link to its field, move focus to it on submit, and mark it as an alert region so it is announced. That serves screen reader and keyboard users, and it also helps everyone on a long form where the first error is off-screen.

question: What accessibility considerations apply to animations?
answer: Respect the reduced motion preference by disabling or simplifying non-essential animation, avoid flashing content that can trigger seizures, keep parallax and auto-playing motion optional, and never convey information by motion alone. A media query check is a few lines and covers most of it.

question: How do you handle a design that is not technically feasible as specified?
answer: Explain the specific constraint - performance, accessibility, platform limitation - propose the closest achievable alternative with a prototype if possible, and involve the designer in the trade-off rather than silently approximating. Silent approximation produces a result nobody signed off and a conversation later.

question: How do you keep implementation faithful to a design system?
answer: Use tokens rather than hard-coded values, build from the shared component library, review visually against the design, and lint for raw colour and spacing values. Faithfulness degrades through small local exceptions, so making the correct path easier than the exception is what maintains it.

question: What should happen when a shared component needs a one-off variation?
answer: Ask whether the variation is general enough to belong in the system; if not, compose around the component or use its provided extension points rather than adding a prop for one consumer. Each single-use prop makes the component harder to change for everyone else.

question: How do you decide whether a performance problem is network or execution?
answer: Look at the waterfall - if time is spent waiting for responses it is network, if the main thread is busy after resources arrive it is execution. They need opposite fixes: fewer or smaller requests versus less or deferred JavaScript. Treating every slowness as a bundle size problem misses half the causes.

question: Why can a fast API still produce a slow page?
answer: Because the request starts late - after the bundle downloads, parses and renders - or because requests are serialised in a waterfall. Total page latency includes when the request was made, not just how long it took, which is why moving fetching to the server or the route level often helps more than optimising the endpoint.

question: How should a form behave when submission fails due to a network error?
answer: Keep the entered data, show a clear retry action, distinguish a network failure from a validation rejection, and avoid disabling the form permanently. Losing a completed form to a transient network problem is among the most damaging experiences an application can produce.

question: What is the right behaviour for a destructive action?
answer: Require confirmation proportional to the consequence, prefer undo over confirmation where the action is reversible, never rely solely on a modal that users dismiss reflexively, and make the confirmation state what will be lost rather than asking are you sure. Undo is better than a dialog for anything that can be reversed.

question: Why can a CSS transition not animate to auto height?
answer: Because the browser cannot interpolate between a length and a keyword, so nothing animates. Workarounds are animating max-height with an estimate, using a grid row template between zero and one fraction, or measuring the content and animating an explicit height - each with its own trade-off.

question: What causes an unexpected horizontal scrollbar?
answer: An element wider than the viewport - usually a fixed width, a long unbreakable string, a negative margin, an absolutely positioned element, or a full-width element inside padded ancestors. Finding it means checking which element's bounding box exceeds the viewport, which developer tools can highlight directly.

question: What is the difference between an iframe and a web component for embedding?
answer: An iframe gives full isolation of styles, scripts and origin, at the cost of communication complexity and layout rigidity. A web component shares the page's context with optional style encapsulation through shadow DOM. Choose an iframe when the embedded content is untrusted or independently deployed.

question: What does shadow DOM encapsulate and what does it not?
answer: It scopes styles and DOM structure so outside CSS does not leak in and internal structure is not selectable from outside. It does not isolate JavaScript, prevent the component from affecting global state, or block inherited properties such as font family - so it is style scoping, not a security boundary.

question: How do you handle a third-party script that degrades performance?
answer: Measure its cost precisely by removing it in a test, load it after interaction or lazily where the vendor supports it, sandbox it in a worker or iframe if possible, and take the measurement to whoever owns the requirement. Vendor scripts are usually added without measurement and removed only with evidence.

question: How do you decide whether a UI problem belongs in the component or the design?
answer: If the behaviour is undefined for a state the design did not consider - an empty list, a very long name, a slow load, an error - that is a design gap, not an implementation detail. Raising it as a design question rather than inventing a behaviour produces a consistent answer across the product.

question: How do you improve interaction responsiveness rather than load performance?
answer: Find the long tasks blocking the main thread during interaction - large re-renders, synchronous work in handlers, expensive layout - and break them up, defer them, or move them off-thread. Load metrics and interaction metrics have different causes, so optimising the bundle rarely improves responsiveness.

question: What causes a flash of unstyled or incorrectly styled content?
answer: Styles arriving after the first paint - render-blocking stylesheets loaded late, CSS-in-JS evaluated after hydration, or a theme applied by JavaScript. Inline the critical styles and apply the theme before paint, since correcting it after the browser has painted is visible regardless of how quickly it happens.

question: How do you handle a browser API that is not universally supported?
answer: Detect it, provide a fallback path or graceful absence of the feature, and check whether the polyfill's cost is justified for the affected share of users. Building a feature that silently does nothing on some browsers is worse than one that visibly offers an alternative.

question: How do you handle a legacy page that must coexist with a new framework?
answer: Mount the new application into a container on the existing page, keep communication to a defined interface such as custom events or a small shared state object, and migrate route by route. Two frameworks controlling the same DOM subtree is the arrangement that produces unexplainable bugs.

question: How do you decide between inline validation and validation on submit?
answer: Validate on blur for format errors so the user is not corrected mid-typing, on submit for cross-field rules, and immediately for irreversible or expensive fields. Validating every keystroke shows errors for input that is merely incomplete, which is the most common frustration in form design.

question: What should happen when a user's session expires mid-task?
answer: Preserve their work locally, prompt to re-authenticate in place rather than redirecting away, and restore them to the same state afterwards. Redirecting to a login page and losing entered data is a common pattern and one of the more damaging experiences an application can produce.

question: How do you handle a page that must display thousands of data points?
answer: Aggregate server-side to the resolution the display can actually show, since a chart cannot render more points than it has pixels. Downsampling with an algorithm that preserves visual shape gives the same appearance at a fraction of the payload and rendering cost.

question: How do you keep a component library's bundle impact reasonable?
answer: Ensure it is tree-shakeable with side-effect-free modules and per-component entry points, avoid a barrel that pulls everything, keep heavy dependencies optional, and measure the cost of importing a single component. A library where one import costs two hundred kilobytes will be avoided by the teams it was built for.

question: How do you debug a style that is being overridden?
answer: Inspect the computed styles panel, which shows which rule won and where the losing rules came from, and check specificity, source order, cascade layer and whether an inline style or important is involved. Guessing at specificity without looking at the computed panel is how the wrong fix is applied.

question: What is the purpose of the loading attribute on images and iframes?
answer: Setting it to lazy defers loading until the element approaches the viewport, reducing initial page weight with no JavaScript. It should not be applied to above-the-fold images, where it delays the largest contentful paint - the common mistake of applying it globally makes the metric worse.

question: How do you handle browser extensions interfering with your application?
answer: Recognise the symptoms - unexplained DOM mutations, hydration mismatches, injected elements - and test in a clean profile to confirm. You cannot control them, so the practical responses are defensive rendering, not assuming exclusive DOM ownership, and asking users to test in a clean profile when reproducing.

question: How do you handle a slow operation that cannot be made faster?
answer: Set expectations with a determinate progress indicator where possible, let the user continue with other work while it runs, notify on completion, and make the wait interruptible. Perceived duration depends more on feedback and control than on the actual time.

question: How do you reduce the cost of a large dependency you cannot remove?
answer: Import only the parts used if it supports it, load it lazily when the feature is reached, replace it for the common case and keep it for the rare one, or move the work server-side. Accepting the cost is also legitimate if measurement shows it is not the constraint.

question: What is the practical difference between session storage and an in-memory variable?
answer: Session storage survives a page refresh and is scoped to the tab; a variable does not survive either. That makes session storage right for state that should persist a reload within a task - a multi-step form's progress - and wrong for anything sensitive, since it is readable by any script on the page.

question: How do you choose between a utility class and a component class?
answer: Utilities for one-off spacing and layout adjustments where naming would add nothing; component classes when the styling represents a reusable concept with meaning. Mixing them deliberately is normal - the failure is either naming every utility or inlining every component's styles as utilities.

question: How do you handle a visual bug that only appears on one device?
answer: Reproduce with remote debugging on the actual device rather than an emulator, check for device-specific rendering behaviour, viewport quirks and font availability, and test the fix on that device. Emulated viewports do not reproduce real rendering engines, which is where such bugs live.

question: How do you decide whether a performance improvement is worth shipping?
answer: By whether it moves a metric users experience by an amount they would notice, measured on representative devices and connections rather than a development machine. A twenty percent improvement in a task that took five milliseconds is not worth added complexity; the same improvement in a two-second interaction is.

question: How do you keep an application's dependencies under control over time?
answer: Review what each dependency provides against its cost periodically, prefer the platform where it has caught up, remove ones used for a single trivial function, and automate updates so staying current is routine. Dependency count grows monotonically unless something deliberately reduces it.

question: What would you check first in a frontend code review for accessibility?
answer: Semantic elements rather than divs with handlers, labels on inputs, keyboard operability of anything interactive, focus handling for dialogs and route changes, and colour contrast. Those five catch the majority of issues and none require specialist tooling to spot.
